<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">(1)&nbsp;&#160; In the fourth quarter
of fiscal 2002, we adopted the Emerging Issues Task Force (EITF) Issue&nbsp;01-14,
&#147;Income Statement Characterization of Reimbursement Received for &#147;Out-of-Pocket&#146;
Expenses Incurred&#148;. Adoption of the EITF Issue&nbsp;01-14 resulted in
reclassifications that increased both revenues and cost of revenues equally by
$13.4&nbsp;million and $10.4&nbsp;million for the years ended May&nbsp;31, 2002,
and May&nbsp;31, 2001, respectively. The change had no effect on net (loss)
income or net (loss) income per share.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">(2)&nbsp;&#160; In fiscal 2002, we
used $10.2&nbsp;million of proceeds from our initial public offering to repay
senior subordinated convertible notes. Due to the repayment of the notes prior
to the scheduled maturity date, we recorded early extinguishment of debt
expense consisting of the unamortized debt issuance costs and the discount on
the notes totaling $2.3&nbsp;million.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">(3)&nbsp;&#160; In fiscal 2002, as a
result of the conversion of the Series&nbsp;A Preferred Stock to common stock,
which accelerated the amortization of the beneficial conversion feature, we
recognized a $30.0&nbsp;million non-cash charge to net income available to</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Business Overview</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">We provide business application software, services and support that
help organizations to manage, analyze and improve their businesses. The markets
we serve include healthcare, retail, financial services (including banking,
insurance and other financial services), local/state government, education and
professional services. We derive revenues from licensing business application
software and providing comprehensive professional services, including consulting,
training and implementation services, as well as ongoing client support and
maintenance. Consulting, training and implementation services are generally not
essential to the functionality of our software products, are sold separately
and also are available from a number of third-party service providers.
Accordingly, revenues from these services are generally recorded separately
from the license fee. We have offices and affiliates serving North and South
America, Europe, Asia, Africa, and Australia.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Challenging
Operating Environment During Fiscal&nbsp;2005</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">&nbsp;</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:35.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">We
continue to face a challenging environment for sales of our software and
services.&#160; Our license fee revenue</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">13</font></p>

<div style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">

<hr size="2" width="100%" noshade color="gray" align="left">

</font></div>

</div>
<!-- SEQ.=1,FOLIO='13',FILE='C:\JMS\eudelhofen\05-13452-1\task513015\13452-1-ba-01.htm',USER='eudelho',CD='Jul 29 15:56 2005' -->


<br clear="all" style="page-break-before:always;">


<div style="font-family:Times New Roman;">

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">declined
year-over-year during the fiscal year ended May&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2005, due to
reduced software demand by our potential and existing clients and increased competition
from Oracle Corporation and SAP AG.We believe the reduced purchasing activity
results from lower capital spending by potential clients for new software
systems, uncertainty among potential clients due to consolidation and other
factors in the software industry, and competing priorities for resources within
our clients such as the recent focus on Sarbanes-Oxley compliance by public
companies.&#160; </font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:35.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Less
new-software licensing activity in fiscal&nbsp;2005 also resulted in fewer
consulting engagement opportunities associated with the implementation of new
software systems, and associated declining professional services revenue during
those periods.&#160; During the fall of&nbsp;2004,
a new leadership team with relevant experience in consulting and services
practices was given responsibility for our professional services. This team has
implemented enhancements to our services, many of which were completed during
the fourth quarter of fiscal&nbsp;2005. Our support revenues increased by $15.8&nbsp;million
during fiscal&nbsp;2005, as compared with prior-year support revenues, due
primarily to the purchase of client maintenance contracts in April&nbsp;2004.
Continued growth in support revenue depends in part on adding new software
clients through licensing activity to offset normal client attrition due to
client consolidation, pricing pressures and other factors.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:35.0pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Critical Accounting Policies and Estimates</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Our discussion and analysis of financial condition and results of
operations are based upon our audited consolidated financial statements, which
have been prepared in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted
in the United States. The preparation of these financial statements requires us
to make estimates and assumptions that affect the reported amounts of assets
and liabilities at the date of the financial statements, the reported amounts
of revenues and expenses during the reporting period, and related disclosures
of contingent assets and liabilities. The Notes to Consolidated Financial
Statements contained herein describe our significant accounting polices used in
the preparation of the consolidated financial statements. On an on-going basis,
we evaluate our estimates, including but not limited to, those related to bad
debt, intangible assets and contingencies. We base our estimates on historical
experience and on various other assumptions that we believe to be reasonable
under the circumstances, the results of which form the basis for making
judgments about the carrying values of assets and liabilities that are not
readily apparent from other sources. Actual results could differ from these
estimates.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">We believe the critical accounting polices listed below reflect our more
significant judgments, estimates and assumptions used in the preparation of our
consolidated financial statements.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Revenue Recognition.</font></i>&#160; Revenue recognition rules&nbsp;for software
companies are very complex. We follow specific and detailed guidelines in determining
the proper amount of revenue to be recorded; however, certain judgments affect
the application of our revenue recognition policy. Revenue results are
difficult to predict, and any shortfall in revenue or delay in recognizing
revenue could cause our operating results to vary significantly from quarter to
quarter.</p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:38.5pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The significant judgments for revenue recognition typically involve
whether collectibility can be considered probable and whether fees are fixed or
determinable. In addition, our transactions often consist of multiple element
arrangements, which must be analyzed to determine the relative fair value of
each element, the amount of revenue to be recognized upon shipment, if any, and
the period and conditions under which deferred revenue should be recognized.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">We recognize revenues in accordance with the provisions of the American
Institute of Certified Public Accountants (&#147;AICPA&#148;) Statement of Position (&#147;SOP&#148;)
97-2, &#147;<i><font style="font-style:italic;">Software Revenue Recognition</font></i>,&#148; as
amended and SOP&nbsp;98-9, &#147;<i><font style="font-style:italic;">Modification of SOP&nbsp;97-2,
Software Revenue Recognition, With Respect to Certain Transactions,</font></i>&#148;
as well as Technical Practice Aids issued from time to time by the AICPA, and
in accordance with the Securities and Exchange Commission Staff Accounting
Bulletin (SAB) No.&nbsp;104, &#147;<i><font style="font-style:italic;">Revenue Recognition.</font></i>&#148;
We license software under non-cancelable license agreements and provide related
professional services, including consulting, training, and implementation
services, as well as ongoing client support and maintenance. Consulting,
training and implementation services are generally not essential to the
functionality of our software products, are sold separately, and also are
available from a number of third-party service providers. Accordingly, revenues
from these services are generally recorded separately from license fees.
Software arrangements including fixed-fee service components are recognized as
the services are performed, while corresponding costs to provide these services
are expensed as incurred. Software arrangements including services that are
essential to the functionality of our software products are recognized using
contract accounting and the&nbsp;percentage-of-completion methodology based on
labor hours input. The amount of judgment involved in addressing significant
assumptions, risks, and uncertainties in applying the application of the&nbsp;percentage-of-completion
methodology can impact the amounts of revenue and related expenses reported in
the consolidated financial statements. Our specific revenue recognition
policies are as follows:</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">14</font></p>

<br clear="all" style="page-break-before:always;">


<div style="font-family:Times New Roman;">

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt .75in;text-autospace:none;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="3" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:12.0pt;">&#149;</font><font size="1" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font><i><font style="font-style:italic;">Software License Fees</font></i>&#151;License
fee revenues from end-users are recognized when the software product has been
shipped, provided a non-cancelable license agreement has been signed, there are
no uncertainties surrounding product acceptance, the fees are fixed or
determinable, and collection of the related receivable is considered probable.
Provided the above criteria are met, license fee revenues from resellers are
recognized when there is a sell-through by a reseller to an end-user. A
sell-through is determined when we receive an order form from a reseller for a
specific end-user sale. We do not generally offer rights of return, acceptance
clauses, or price protection to our clients. In situations where we do provide
rights of return or acceptance clauses, revenue is deferred until the clause
expires. Typically, our software license fees are due within a twelve-month
period from the date of shipment. If the fee due from the client is not fixed
or determinable, including payment terms greater than twelve months from
shipment, revenue is recognized as payments become due and all other conditions
for revenue recognition have been satisfied. In software arrangements that
include rights to multiple software products, specified upgrades, maintenance
or services, we allocate the total arrangement fee among each deliverable using
the fair value of each of the deliverables determined using vendor-specific
objective evidence. Vendor-specific objective evidence of fair value is
determined using the price charged when that element is sold separately. In
software arrangements in which we have fair value of all undelivered elements
but not of a delivered element, we use the residual method to record revenue.
Under the residual method, the fair value of the undelivered elements is
deferred and the remaining portion of the arrangement fee is allocated to the
delivered element(s) and is recognized as revenue. In software arrangements in
which we do not have vendor-specific objective evidence of fair value of all
undelivered elements, revenue is deferred until fair value is determined or all
elements for which we do not have vendor-specific objective evidence of fair
value, have been delivered.</p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .75in;text-autospace:none;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt .75in;text-autospace:none;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="3" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:12.0pt;">&#149;</font><font size="1" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font><i><font style="font-style:italic;">Services</font></i>&#151;Revenues
from training and consulting services are recognized as services are provided
to clients. Revenues from maintenance contracts are recognized ratably over the
term of the maintenance agreements. Revenues for client support and maintenance
that are bundled with the initial license fee are deferred based on the fair
value of the bundled support services and recognized ratably over the term of
the agreement. Fair value is based on the renewal rate for continued support
arrangements.</p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Allowance for Doubtful Accounts.</font></i>&#160; We maintain an allowance for doubtful
accounts at an amount we estimate to be sufficient to provide adequate
protection against losses resulting from extending credit to our clients. In
judging the adequacy of the allowance for doubtful accounts, we consider multiple
factors including historical bad debt experience, the general economic
environment, the need for specific client reserves and the aging of our
receivables. This provision is included in operating expenses as a general and
administrative expense. A considerable amount of judgment is required in
assessing these factors. If the factors utilized in determining the allowance
do not reflect future performance, then a change in the allowance for doubtful
accounts would be necessary in the period such determination has been made
impacting future results of operations.</p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:38.5pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:38.5pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Sales Returns and Allowances.</font></i>&#160; Although we do not provide a contractual
right of return, in the course of arriving at practical business solutions to
various warranty and other claims, we have allowed sales returns and
allowances. We record a provision for estimated sales returns and allowances on
license in the same period the related revenues are recorded or when current
information indicates additional amounts are required. These estimates are
based on historical experience determined by analysis of specific return
activity and other known factors. If the historical data we utilize does not
reflect future performance, then a change in the allowances would be necessary
in the period such determination has been made impacting future results of
operations.</p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Valuation of Long-Lived and Intangible Assets
and Goodwill.</font></i>&#160;
We review identifiable intangible and other long-lived assets for
impairment whenever events or changes in circumstances indicate the carrying
amount may not be recoverable. Events or changes in circumstances that indicate
the carrying amount may not be recoverable include, but are not limited to, a
significant decrease in the market value of the business or asset acquired, a
significant adverse change in the extent or manner in which the business or
asset acquired is used or a significant adverse change in the business climate.
If such events or changes in circumstances are present, the undiscounted cash
flows method is used to determine whether the long-lived asset is impaired.
Cash flows would include the estimated terminal value of the asset and exclude
any interest charges. To the extent the carrying value of the asset exceeds the
undiscounted cash flows over the estimated remaining life of the asset, the
impairment is measured using the discounted cash flows. The discount rate
utilized would be based on management&#146;s best estimate of the related risks and
return at the time the impairment assessment is made.</p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">15</font></p>

<div style="font-family:Times New Roman;">

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:38.5pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">If such events or changes in circumstances are present, the first step
of the goodwill impairment test, used to identify potential impairment,
compares the fair value of a reporting unit with its carrying amount, including
goodwill. We operate as one reporting unit and therefore compare our book value
to market value. Market value is determined utilizing our market capitalization
plus a control premium. If our market value exceeds our book value, goodwill is
considered not impaired, thus the second step of the impairment test is not
necessary. If our book value exceeds our market value, the second step of the
goodwill impairment test is performed to measure the amount of impairment loss,
if any. The second step of the goodwill impairment test, used to measure the
amount of impairment loss, compares the implied fair value of the goodwill with
the book value of the goodwill. If the carrying value of the goodwill exceeds
the implied fair value of the goodwill, an impairment loss would be recognized
in an amount equal to the excess. Any loss recognized cannot exceed the
carrying amount of goodwill. After a goodwill impairment loss is recognized,
the adjusted carrying amount of goodwill is the new accounting basis. A
subsequent reversal of a previously recognized goodwill impairment loss is
prohibited once the measurement of that loss is completed.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:38.5pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In accordance with SFAS No.&nbsp;144 &#147;<i><font style="font-style:italic;">Accounting for the Impairment or Disposal of Long-Lived Assets</font></i>&#148;,
we review long-lived assets for impairment whenever events or changes in
circumstances indicate the carrying amount may not be recoverable. Events or
changes in circumstances that indicate the carrying amount may not be
recoverable include, but are not limited to, a significant decrease in the market
value of the business or asset acquired, a significant adverse change in the
extent or manner in which the business or asset acquired is used or a
significant adverse change in the business climate. If such events or changes
in circumstances are present, the undiscounted cash flows method is used to
determine whether the asset is impaired. Cash flows would include the estimated
terminal value of the asset and exclude any interest charges. To the extent the
carrying value of the asset exceeds the undiscounted cash flows over the
estimated remaining life of the asset, the impairment is measured using the
discounted cash flows. The discount rate utilized would be based on management&#146;s
best estimate of the related risks and return at the time the impairment assessment
is made.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:38.5pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Deferred Taxes.</font></i>&#160; Significant judgment is required in
determining our income taxes in each of the jurisdictions in which we operate.
This process involves estimating our actual current tax exposure together with
assessing temporary differences resulting from differing treatment of items for
tax and financial reporting purposes. These differences result in deferred tax
assets and liabilities, which are included within our consolidated balance
sheets. Although we believe our assessments are reasonable, no assurance can be
given that the final tax outcome of these matters will not be different than
that which is reflected in our historical income tax provisions, benefits and
accruals. Such differences could have a material effect on our income tax
provision and net income in the period in which such a determination is made.</p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:38.5pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">We must assess the likelihood that our net deferred tax assets will be
recovered from future taxable income and to the extent we believe that recovery
is not likely, we must establish a valuation allowance. To the extent we
establish a valuation allowance we must include an expense within the tax
provision in the statement of operations. As of May&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2005, and May&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2004,
the consolidated balance sheets include net deferred tax assets in the amount
of $30.7&nbsp;million and $27.7&nbsp;million, respectively. These amounts are
reported net of any accumulated valuation allowance.&nbsp;For the year ended
May&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2005, we established a valuation allowance through the
provision for income taxes of $0.4&nbsp;million for certain deferred tax assets
associated with federal contributing carryforwards and state net operating loss
carryforwards. For the year ended May&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2004, we recorded a
valuation allowance through the provision for income taxes of $1.2&nbsp;million
for federal contribution carryforwards, tax credit carryforwards,&nbsp;and
state net operating loss carryforwards.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">We have established a full valuation allowance against our foreign tax
operating losses, because it was determined that they are not likely to be
realized. As of May&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2005, we recorded an accumulated valuation
allowance of $20.0&nbsp;million against these losses.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Our methodology for determining the realizability of our deferred tax
assets involves estimates of future taxable income from our core business, the
estimated impact of future stock option deductions from outstanding stock
options, and the expiration dates and amounts of net operating loss
carryforwards and other tax credits. These estimates are projected through the
life of the related deferred tax assets based on assumptions which management
believes to be reasonable and consistent with current operating results.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Although we had cumulative pre-tax income for financial reporting
purposes for the three years ended May&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2005, we did not pay any
significant income taxes over that period because tax deductions from the
exercise of stock options granted prior to our initial public offering
generated tax operating losses for the years ended May&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2005,&nbsp;2004
and 2003. In assessing the realizability of our deferred tax assets as of May&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2005,
we considered evidence regarding our ability to generate sufficient future
taxable income to realize our deferred tax assets. The primary evidence
considered included the cumulative tax operating loss for the past three years;
the cumulative pre-tax income for financial reporting purposes for the past
three years; the estimated impact of future tax deductions from the exercise of
stock options outstanding as of </font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">May&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2005; and the estimated future taxable income based

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">We estimate, based largely
on historical income, that it may take 10&nbsp;years or more before we fully

we concluded that it was more likely than not that tax loss carryforwards and

carryforwards and state net operating loss carryforwards.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">We also concluded that it was more likely than not that the net
deferred tax assets of $30.7&nbsp;million as of May&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2005, as well

in greater than ten years. Based on this conclusion, we would require
approximately $110.2&nbsp;million in cumulative future taxable income to be
generated at various times over the next twenty years to realize the related
net deferred tax assets of $30.7&nbsp;million as of May&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2005, as
well as the estimated future tax deductions from the exercise of stock options
outstanding&#160; as of May&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2005.
Additionally, we determined that it is likely the net deferred tax assets will
continue to increase for the next several years prior to utilization of the tax
loss carryforwards and could increase in excess of $20.6&nbsp;million if the
stock options outstanding as of May&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2005 are exercised.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In the event that we adjust estimates of future taxable income or tax
deductions from the exercise of stock options, or our stock price increases
significantly without a corresponding increase in taxable income, we may need
to establish an additional valuation allowance, which could materially impact our
financial position and results of operations.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Contingencies.</font></i>&#160; We are subject to the possibility of various
loss contingencies in the normal course of business. We accrue for
contingencies when a loss is probable and can be reasonably estimated.</p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Informal Securities and Exchange Commission Investigation</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">&nbsp;</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:35.3pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On
January&nbsp;5,&nbsp;2005, we announced that the Securities and Exchange
Commission (SEC) conducted an informal investigation concerning our revenue
recognition practices. We have fully cooperated with the SEC. In response to a
telephone call from the SEC seeking information from us, our Audit Committee
retained independent legal counsel, which retained an independent accounting
firm, to investigate thoroughly the issues identified by the SEC. The Audit
Committee&#146;s investigation was completed in January&nbsp;2005. Following the
Audit Committee&#146;s investigation, we concluded that our financial statements can
continue to be relied upon and need not be restated. The Audit Committee shared
the results of its independent investigation with the SEC in early January&nbsp;2005.
We have not received further communication from the SEC since we shared our
results of the investigation in January&nbsp;2005. The SEC is not bound by the
results of our independent investigation.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:35.3pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">We
incurred $2.7&nbsp;million in fees and expenses for this independent
investigation in fiscal&nbsp;2005. If the SEC initiates a formal investigation
or initiates other actions, we would incur additional fees and expenses and may
incur other associated costs or liabilities.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Purchase of Client Maintenance Contracts</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On April&nbsp;30,&nbsp;2004, we acquired assets consisting of client
maintenance contracts and client lists from Siemens Medical Solutions Health
Services Corporation (&#147;Siemens&#148;) for $19.8&nbsp;million in cash and $4.3&nbsp;million
in other consideration. Of the total purchase price, $22.9&nbsp;million was
allocated to the maintenance contracts and is being amortized over the
remaining life of the contracts based on estimated periodic contractual revenue
recognized. The purchase price allocated to the client list of $1.0&nbsp;million
is being amortized on a straight-line basis over 7&nbsp;years. The remaining
purchase price of $0.2&nbsp;million in transitional support costs was charged
to cost of services as the services were performed in&nbsp;2004.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The asset purchase agreement was part of an overall restructuring of a
10-year partner agreement between us and Siemens. As part of the agreement,
Siemens became our preferred partner for hosting our software applications
within the United States healthcare market, and we became Siemens&#146; preferred
Enterprise Resource Planning (&#147;ERP&#148;) software vendor for healthcare. Under the
asset purchase agreement, we assumed responsibility for supporting clients who
use our software applications previously supported by Siemens. The asset
purchase agreement did not qualify as a business combination under the criteria
established in Statement of Financial Accounting Standards (SFAS)&nbsp;No.&nbsp;141,
&#147;<i><font style="font-style:italic;">Business Combinations</font></i>&#148;.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">17</font></p>

<div>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Acquisitions</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On June&nbsp;2,&nbsp;2005, we announced that
we had entered into an agreement to combine with Stockholm, Sweden-based
Intentia International AB (&#147;Intentia&#148;) in an all-stock transaction. We plan to
affect the business combination through a recommended public offer in Sweden
for (i)&nbsp;all outstanding Intentia Series&nbsp;A and Series&nbsp;B shares
and (ii)&nbsp;all outstanding warrants to purchase Series&nbsp;B shares, in
each case in exchange for shares of our Common Stock. The transaction is
expected to be completed in the second or third quarter of fiscal 2006 subject
to, among other things, shareholder, regulatory and public authority approvals
and sufficient tender of shares by Intentia stockholders. The transaction is
expected to be accounted for under the purchase method of accounting. Refer to
Footnote 18, &#147;Subsequent Events&#148; in the notes to the Consolidated Financial
Statements for additional information.&#160; </font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The following acquisitions were accounted for under the purchase method
of accounting. Accordingly, the assets and liabilities acquired were recorded
at their estimated fair values at the effective date of the acquisition and the
results of operations have been included in the audited consolidated statements
of operations since the acquisition date. In accordance with Statement of
Financial Accounting Standards (&#147;SFAS&#148;) No.&nbsp;142, &#147;<i><font style="font-style:italic;">Goodwill and
Other Intangible Assets</font></i>,&#148; goodwill recorded as a result of these
acquisitions is subject to an annual impairment test and is not amortized.
These acquisitions are intended to enhance our focus on targeted vertical
markets and to provide additional value-added products and services to our
clients.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On October&nbsp;15, 2003, we acquired all of the outstanding capital
stock of Apexion for $8.0&nbsp;million in cash, net of cash acquired. Terms of
the initial agreement provide for additional cash payments ranging from zero to
$2.0&nbsp;million, contingent upon the future performance of Apexion measured
annually through November&nbsp;30,&nbsp;2005. As of May&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2005, no
additional consideration had been earned or recorded under this agreement.
Apexion provided materials and equipment logistics solutions for the healthcare
industry.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On September&nbsp;30, 2003, we acquired all of the outstanding capital
stock of Closedloop for $4.2&nbsp;million in cash, net of cash acquired.
Closedloop provided collaborative budgeting, planning and forecasting solutions
using real-time, transactional functionality.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On July&nbsp;24, 2003, we acquired all of the outstanding capital stock
of Numbercraft for $3.7&nbsp;million in cash, net of cash acquired and $0.3&nbsp;million
in notes payable. Terms of the initial agreement provide for additional cash
payments ranging from zero to $9.0&nbsp;million contingent upon the future
performance of Numbercraft measured periodically through fiscal 2007. Any
contingent consideration earned is recorded as additional goodwill. During the
fiscal years ended May&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2005 and May&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2004, $0.5&nbsp;million
and $1.1&nbsp;million of additional consideration was earned and recorded as
additional goodwill, respectively. This amount and certain elements of the
initial purchase price have been included in notes payable to the former
principals of Numbercraft. As of May&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2005, the remaining
potential contingent consideration was approximately $5.9&nbsp;million.
Numbercraft provided solutions for retailers and consumer packaged goods
companies, which enable a quantitative understanding of consumer dynamics,
product and offer performance, and client trends.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On June&nbsp;28, 2002, we acquired certain assets of Armature
Holdings&nbsp;Ltd. for $7.8&nbsp;million in cash, net of cash acquired.
Acquired assets included all software applications, related trademarks and
technologies. Armature provided merchandising/category management and supply
chain management solutions for retailers, consumer goods manufacturers, and
wholesalers.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Fiscal Year Ended May&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2005 Compared
With Fiscal Year Ended May&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2004</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Revenues</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:38.5pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Total Revenues.</font></i>&#160; We license software under non-cancelable
license agreements and provide related professional services including
consulting, training, and implementation services, as well as ongoing client
support and maintenance. Total revenues decreased to $335.2&nbsp;million in
fiscal&nbsp;2005 from $363.6&nbsp;million in fiscal&nbsp;2004, or 7.8%. The $28.4&nbsp;million
decline in total revenue was attributed to a $34.6&nbsp;million decrease in
license fees partially offset by a $6.2&nbsp;million increase in services
revenues.</p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:38.5pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:38.5pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">License Fees.</font></i>&#160; Revenues from license fees decreased to $57.7&nbsp;million
in fiscal&nbsp;2005 from $92.3&nbsp;million in fiscal&nbsp;2004, or 37.5%. The
$34.6&nbsp;million decline in license
fees was primarily due to a reduction in new and existing client business
activity due to continued consolidation and uncertainty in the industry, as
well as competing priorities such as Sarbanes-Oxley compliance by public
companies, reducing capital spending on software. The average overall selling
price of our licensing transactions in fiscal&nbsp;2005 decreased 23.5%, while
the number of licensing transactions decreased 18.1%, as compared to fiscal&nbsp;2004.
Revenues from license fees as a&nbsp;percentage of total revenues, for fiscal&nbsp;2005
and fiscal&nbsp;2004, were 17.2% and 25.4%, respectively. &#160;</p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:38.5pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Services.</font></i>&#160; Service revenues consist of consulting,
maintenance and training services provided to clients. Revenues from services increased to $277.4&nbsp;million for fiscal&nbsp;2005
from $271.2&nbsp;million for fiscal&nbsp;2004, representing an increase of 2.3%.
The $6.2&nbsp;million increase in services was due to a $15.8&nbsp;million
increase in support revenue that was partially offset by</p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">19</font></p>

<br clear="all" style="page-break-before:always;">


<div style="font-family:Times New Roman;">

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">a $9.6&nbsp;million decrease in consulting revenue. The $15.8&nbsp;million
increase in support revenue was primarily due to a $10.1&nbsp;million increase
in revenue earned on support contracts purchased in April&nbsp;2004, and a $4.5&nbsp;million
increase in revenue primarily related to price increases. The $9.6&nbsp;million
decrease in consulting revenue was due to lower business activity in product
sales that directly impacts consulting revenue combined with increased
competitive pricing pressures. Services revenues as a&nbsp;percentage of total
revenues for fiscal&nbsp;2005 and&nbsp;2004 were 82.8% and 74.6%, respectively.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Cost of Revenues</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Cost of License Fees.</font></i>&#160; Cost
of license fees includes royalties to third parties, amortization of acquired
software, and software delivery expenses. Our software solutions may include
embedded components of third-party vendors, for which a fee is paid to the
vendor upon the sale of our products. In addition, we resell third-party
products in conjunction with the license of our software solutions. The cost of
license fees is higher when we resell products of third-party vendors. As a
result, gross margins vary depending on the proportion of third-party product
sales in our revenue mix. </p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Cost of license fees decreased to $10.0&nbsp;million for fiscal&nbsp;2005
from $15.9&nbsp;million for fiscal&nbsp;2004, representing a decrease of 37.5%.&#160; The $5.9&nbsp;million decrease was primarily
due to a 37.5% decline in license fees which included a decline in the
proportion of third-party product sales in our revenue mix. Cost of license
fees as a&nbsp;percentage of total revenues for fiscal&nbsp;2005 and fiscal&nbsp;2004
were 3.0% and 4.4%, respectively. Gross margin on revenue from license fees was
82.7% for fiscal&nbsp;2005 and fiscal&nbsp;2004.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></i></p>

<p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Cost of Services.</font></i> &#160;Cost
of services includes salaries, employee benefits, and related travel and
overhead costs for providing consulting, training, implementation and support
services to clients, as well as intangible asset amortization on support
contracts purchased in April&nbsp;2004. Cost of services increased to $140.6&nbsp;million
for fiscal&nbsp;2005 from $136.3&nbsp;million for fiscal&nbsp;2004 representing
an increase of 3.2%. The $4.3&nbsp;million increase was primarily due to a $5.0&nbsp;million
increase in third-party consulting costs resulting from a higher proportion of
third-party services in our revenue mix, and a $3.7&nbsp;million increase in
amortization related to support contracts purchased in April&nbsp;2004. These
increases were partially offset by a $1.9&nbsp;million decrease in travel
related costs; a $0.9&nbsp;million decrease in employee related costs,
including a $2.1&nbsp;million decrease due to the favorable impacts from
restructuring activities, and a $0.6&nbsp;million reduction in incentive
compensation, partially offset by a $2.0&nbsp;million increase in annual salaries
due to merit increases; a $0.6&nbsp;million decrease due to general cost
control activities; and a $0.4&nbsp;million decrease in our annual reward
program. Cost of services as a&nbsp;percentage of total revenues for fiscal&nbsp;2005
and fiscal&nbsp;2004 were 41.9% and 37.5%, respectively.&#160; Gross margin on services revenues were 49.3%
and 49.8% for fiscal&nbsp;2005 and fiscal&nbsp;2004, respectively.</p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Operating Expenses</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></i></b></p>

<p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:38.5pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Research and Development.</font></i>&#160;
Research and development expenses consist primarily of salaries,
employee benefits, related overhead costs, and consulting fees associated with
product development, enhancements, upgrades, testing, quality assurance, and
documentation. Research and development expenses decreased to $62.2&nbsp;million
for fiscal&nbsp;2005 from $64.9&nbsp;million for fiscal&nbsp;2004, representing
a decrease of 4.2%. The $2.7&nbsp;million decrease in research and development
was primarily due to a $4.3&nbsp;million reduction in employee related costs,
including a $1.7&nbsp;million decrease in salaries due to the favorable impacts
from restructuring activities, a $2.0&nbsp;million decrease in incentive
compensation, and a $1.5&nbsp;million decrease due to a reduction in headcount,
partially offset by a $1.3&nbsp;million increase in annual salaries; and a $1.0&nbsp;million
decrease in other development activities. These decreases were partially offset
by a $2.9&nbsp;million increase in spending on corporate initiatives, including
$1.9&nbsp;million related to the third-party offshore software support services
agreement we entered into in February&nbsp;2004. Research and development
expenses as a&nbsp;percentage of total revenues for fiscal&nbsp;2005 and fiscal&nbsp;2004
were 18.5% and 17.8%, respectively.</p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:38.5pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Sales and Marketing.</font></i>&#160; Sales
and marketing expenses consist primarily of salaries and incentive compensation,
employee benefits, travel, and overhead costs related to our sales and
marketing personnel, as well as trade show activities, advertising costs, and
other costs associated with marketing our company. &#160;Sales and marketing expenses decreased to $75.6&nbsp;million
for fiscal&nbsp;2005 from $93.1&nbsp;million for fiscal&nbsp;2004, representing
a decrease of 18.8%.</p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

$17.5&nbsp;million decrease in sales and marketing expenses was primarily due
to a $12.6&nbsp;million decrease in employee related costs, including a $5.9&nbsp;million
decrease in incentive compensation, and a $3.4&nbsp;million decrease in
salaries due to the favorable impacts resulting from restructuring activities;
a decrease of $1.7&nbsp;million in payroll taxes and benefits and a </font></p>

<div style="font-family:Times New Roman;">

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">$1.2&nbsp;million
decrease due to a reduction in headcount; and a $4.8&nbsp;million decrease due
to general cost containment activities, primarily travel related costs. Sales
and marketing expenses as a&nbsp;percentage of total revenues for fiscal&nbsp;2005
and fiscal&nbsp;2004 were 22.6% and 25.6%, respectively.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">General and Administrative.</font></i>&#160;
General and administrative expenses consist primarily of salaries,
employee benefits and related overhead costs for administrative employees, as
well as legal and accounting expenses, consulting fees and bad debt expense. General
and administrative expenses decreased to $36.4&nbsp;million for fiscal&nbsp;2005
from $37.7&nbsp;million for fiscal&nbsp;2004, representing a decrease of 3.4%.</p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The
$1.3&nbsp;million decrease in general and administrative expenses was primarily
due to a $2.2&nbsp;million decline in bad debt expense due primarily to the
favorable impacts from focused collection efforts, a client settlement and a general
decrease in revenues; and a $2.5&nbsp;million decrease in other legal related
costs. There was a $1.5&nbsp;million decrease in employee related costs,
including a $2.1&nbsp;million decrease in incentive compensation; and a $0.5&nbsp;million
decrease due to the favorable impacts of restructuring activities, partially
offset by a $1.0&nbsp;million increase in salaries; and a $0.9&nbsp;million decrease
in foreign currency transactions. These decreases were partially offset by a $2.7&nbsp;million
in fees and expenses related to the SEC&#146;s informal investigation, $2.5&nbsp;million
in costs associated with Sarbanes-Oxley compliance initiatives, and a $0.8&nbsp;million
increase due to corporate initiatives designed to increase efficiencies. General
and administrative expenses as a&nbsp;percentage of total revenues for fiscal&nbsp;2005
and fiscal&nbsp;2004 were 10.9% and 10.4%, respectively.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Restructuring. </font></i>&#160;During fiscal&nbsp;2005 we recorded $5.0&nbsp;million
of restructuring charges, net of reversals, related to corporate restructuring
initiatives. </p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On
September&nbsp;28,&nbsp;2004, we approved a plan designed to enhance the
Company&#146;s operating effectiveness and profitability. Under the restructuring
plan (Phase I), we streamlined structure, consolidated leadership and reduced
long-term costs to realign projected expenses with anticipated revenue levels.
The plan included the reduction of 107 employees in the United States and the
United Kingdom, which in accordance with SFAS No.&nbsp;112, <i><font style="font-style:italic;">Employers Accounting for Post Employment Benefits - an amendment of
FASB Statements No.&nbsp;5 and 43</font></i>, resulted in a charge for
severance and related benefits of $2.9&nbsp;million, net of a reversal of $0.03&nbsp;million
subsequent to the initial charge in the year ended May&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2005. The
reduction included employees who worked in operations, marketing, sales,
research and development, maintenance and services. Cash payments during fiscal&nbsp;2005
for the Phase I plan were $2.9&nbsp;million. All employee reductions and
related cash payments were substantially completed as of May&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2005.
The remaining cash payments are expected to be completed during fiscal 2006.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">At
November&nbsp;30,&nbsp;2004, we also accrued for a plan (Phase II) that included
initiatives to further reduce costs and realign projected expenses with
anticipated revenue levels. It included a reduction of 68 employees in the
United States and the United Kingdom, and because we were able to determine
probability at the end of the second quarter of fiscal&nbsp;2005, the
restructuring plan resulted in a charge of approximately $2.2&nbsp;million, net
of a reversal of $0.3&nbsp;million subsequent to the initial charge for
severance and related benefits, in accordance with SFAS No.&nbsp;112. The
reduction included employees who worked in sales, research and development and
services. Cash payments during fiscal&nbsp;2005 for the Phase II plan were $2.0&nbsp;million.
All employee reductions and related cash payments were substantially completed
as of May&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2005. The remaining cash payments are expected to be
completed during fiscal 2006.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">During
fiscal&nbsp;2005, we experienced a reduction in our fully burdened employee
related costs of approximately $9.9&nbsp;million due to our fiscal&nbsp;2005
restructuring activities. As a result of our fiscal&nbsp;2005 restructuring
plans, beginning in fiscal 2006 and going forward we anticipate an annualized
reduction in our employee related costs of approximately $19.0&nbsp;million.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">As
of May&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2005, remaining reserve balances related to prior years&#146; restructurings
consist of $0.6&nbsp;million in employee related costs and $0.03&nbsp;million
of facility closure liabilities. Although the restructuring plans for fiscal&nbsp;2004,
2003 and 2002 have been fully executed, we continue to make cash payments for
continuing lease and employee related costs. During fiscal&nbsp;2005, we made
cash payments totaling $0.2&nbsp;million. The remaining cash payments for the
prior years&#146; restructurings are expected to be completed during fiscal 2006.</font></p>

to $1.5&nbsp;million for fiscal&nbsp;2005 from $1.3&nbsp;million for fiscal&nbsp;2004.
The $0.2&nbsp;million increase in amortization expense primarily reflects the

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Other Income, net</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Other income, net which is comprised of interest income earned from
cash, marketable securities and long term investments, was $4.3&nbsp;million
for fiscal&nbsp;2005 compared with $3.2&nbsp;million for fiscal&nbsp;2004. The increase
in interest income was primarily due to an increase in the average yield on
investments compared with the same prior-year period, partially offset by an
approximate $20.9&nbsp;million decrease in average invested balances compared with
the same prior year period.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Provision (Benefit)
for Income Taxes</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-indent:38.5pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Our provision for income taxes for fiscal&nbsp;2005 was $2.9&nbsp;million,
compared to $7.3&nbsp;million for fiscal&nbsp;2004.&#160; This decrease in income tax expense was due
to a decrease in income before income taxes and a decrease in our effective
income tax rate.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-indent:38.5pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-indent:38.5pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Our effective income tax
rate for fiscal&nbsp;2005 was 35.2%, compared to 47.8% for fiscal&nbsp;2004.&#160; This decrease in our effective tax rate was
due primarily to increased tax benefits as a&nbsp;percentage of income before
income taxes from research and development tax credits and tax-exempt
income.&#160; Additionally, a decrease in the
change in the valuation allowance related to state and federal tax
carryforwards contributed to the decrease in the effective tax rate.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-indent:38.5pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-indent:38.5pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Our annual effective tax
rate may fluctuate from year to year due primarily to changes in the amount and
mix of domestic and foreign income, changes in our estimates of federal tax
credits, tax deductions, and tax-exempt income, changes in our valuation
allowance related to deferred tax assets, and changes in tax legislation.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-indent:38.5pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-indent:38.5pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">During fiscal years&nbsp;2005
and&nbsp;2004, we recorded income tax benefits of $4.2&nbsp;million and $11.6&nbsp;million,
respectively, related to deductions for employee stock option exercises. This
tax benefit, which decreased current income taxes payable and decreased
additional paid-in capital by equal amounts, had no effect on our provision for
income taxes.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-indent:38.5pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Fiscal Year Ended May&nbsp;31,&nbsp;2004 Compared
With Fiscal Year Ended May&nbsp;31, 2003</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Revenues</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-indent:38.5pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Total Revenues.</font></i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160; Total
revenues increased to $363.6&nbsp;million in fiscal&nbsp;2004 from $344.3&nbsp;million
in fiscal 2003, or 5.6%. The $19.3&nbsp;million increase in total revenues was
attributed to a $14.7&nbsp;million increase in license fees and a $4.5&nbsp;million
increase in services revenues.</font><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160; </font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-indent:.5in;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">License Fees.</font></i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;
Revenues from license fees increased to $92.3&nbsp;million in fiscal&nbsp;2004
from $77.6&nbsp;million in fiscal 2003, representing an increase of 19.0%. The
$14.7&nbsp;million increase in license fees was due to improvements in market
conditions in the most recent six months compared with last year, which improved
the level of information technology spending. </font><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The average overall selling price of our
licensing transactions increased 5.5%, while the number of licensing
transactions decreased 1.1% as compared with fiscal 2003. </font><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Revenues
from license fees as a&nbsp;percentage of total revenues for fiscal&nbsp;2004
were 25.4%, compared with 22.5% in fiscal 2003, reflecting the increase in
license fees in proportion to revenues from services.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Services.</font></i>&#160; Revenues from services increased to $271.2&nbsp;million
for fiscal&nbsp;2004 from $266.7&nbsp;million in fiscal 2003, representing an
increase of 1.7%. The $4.5&nbsp;million increase in services was due to a $12.3&nbsp;million
increase in support revenue that was partially offset by a $7.8&nbsp;million decrease
in consulting revenue. The $12.3&nbsp;million increase in support revenue was
primarily due to an expanded client base from new licensing activity since the
prior year period combined with price increases. The $7.8&nbsp;million decrease
in consulting revenue was primarily due to the decline in new license activity
in fiscal 2003, which resulted in fewer consulting and training opportunities
in fiscal&nbsp;2004. New consulting and training opportunities typically lagged
behind new licensing activity by several quarters. Services revenues as a&nbsp;percentage
of total revenues for fiscal&nbsp;2004 and 2003 were 74.6% and 77.5%,
respectively.</p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Cost of Revenues</font></i></b></p>

<p style="font-size:10.0pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;text-indent:.5in;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Cost of License Fees.</font></i>&#160; Cost of license fees increased to $15.9&nbsp;million
for fiscal&nbsp;2004 from $14.4&nbsp;million for fiscal 2003, representing an
increase of 11.0%. The $1.5&nbsp;million increase in cost of license fees was
primarily due to a $1.2&nbsp;million increase in amortization of acquired
software related to our acquisitions, and a $0.2&nbsp;million increase in third-party
costs. Cost of license fees as a&nbsp;percentage of total revenues for fiscal&nbsp;2004
and 2003 was 4.4% and 4.2%, respectively. Gross margin on</p>
